This case highlights that "Uptime Ransom" is now a standard threat even for traditional, non-tech manufacturing sectors. The AlphV/BlackCat group claimed responsibility on August 2, 2023, alleging access to sensitive executive data. The company engaged forensic experts, notified law enforcement, and resumed operations while investigating potential data theft.

A billion-dollar boating manufacturing firm, Brunswick Corporation, suffered a cyberattack in June 2023 that not only disrupted operations for 9 days but also cost the organization $85 million. In addition, the firm filed a notice with the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office that the breach compromised the personal information of employees and customers, including names, mailing addresses, Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, payment card data, and health information.

As a multi-billion-dollar organization that supplies semiconductor technology to a number of partners, Applied Materials is a good example of supply chain risk. It became the victim of a supply-chain ransomware attack in February 2023 that disrupted shipments, and while not confirmed, it’s been reported that MKS Instruments is the main victim of this attack, according to Bloomberg. The cost of $250 million is said to be from lost sales in the second quarter of 2023, following the breach. As organizations become more connected, especially in the manufacturing sector, these kinds of attacks have increased, as threat actors seek out weak points in the supply chain.

Incident Name: Clorox Manufacturing — Social Engineering to Shopfloor
Verified Impact Summary: Scattered Spider social-engineered a service desk into resetting passwords, then moved laterally from IT into Clorox’s operational backbone. Manufacturing was disrupted for months. Direct costs: $49M. Total losses including lost revenue: $380M. The lesson: OT security starts at the help desk.

Simpson Manufacturing Company, a manufacturer of building materials, was the victim of a cyber attack in October 2023 that caused it to take systems offline, disrupting business operations. The systems remained down as of December 2023, highlighting the severe scope of the incident. While it’s unknown if the root cause was ransomware, it’s been reported that the incident response steps are like that seen in ransomware attacks. The disruption caused the public company’s stock to decline by 9.4% over a single month.

ABB, a Swiss-Swedish multinational and one of the "Big Four" in industrial automation, suffered a massive ransomware attack by the Black Basta group. The attack hit the company’s internal Windows Active Directory, which is the "nerve center" for managing employee and engineer access. ABB had to terminate VPN connections with its customers to prevent the malware from "island hopping" into the factories of its clients (which include global power grids and manufacturing plants). It was a chilling reminder that an attack on an automation provider is a threat to every factory they support.

On January 30, 2025, Unimicron Technology reported a cyberattack affecting its IT systems in China. The previously little-known Sarcoma ransomware group claimed responsibility, listing the company on its leak site on February 11, 2025. The group claimed to have stolen approximately 377GB of data, including SQL files and internal documents, threatening a double-extortion leak. Unimicron engaged external forensic experts and stated the operational impact was initially limited, although data theft was confirmed by the attacker.

Foxconn’s subsidiary, which focuses on critical connectors and cables for the global tech supply chain, suffered a major data breach by the INC_RANSOM group. The group successfully exfiltrated a massive dataset and threatened to leak the technical designs of proprietary connector technologies used by major smartphone and EV manufacturers. The breach caused a 48-hour "precautionary" shutdown of several assembly lines in Southeast Asia. This incident served as a stark reminder of how sub-tier component manufacturers (Tier 2 and Tier 3) are now viewed by hackers as the most efficient way to disrupt global "just-in-time" production schedules.

India’s largest cable manufacturer, Polycab India Ltd, suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted internal files and disrupted operations, causing ₹20 crore (~$2.4M) in operational losses. The attack started with an infected employee workstation and moved laterally through flat network architecture — a scenario replicated across thousands of Indian manufacturing SMEs.

In May, Nucor Corporation, the largest U.S. steelmaker, reported a cyberattack involving unauthorized access to IT systems, which forced a temporary halt in some production operations. To protect its network and contain the incident, Nucor was forced to temporarily shut down some production facilities. he breach prompted a forensic investigation, and the company immediately initiated safety protocols to bring systems back online securely. This attack highlighted vulnerabilities in high-value, critical infrastructure manufacturing within the US.

Verified Impact Summary: Between March and June 2025, Chinese-aligned threat actors ramped up coordinated cyber espionage campaigns targeting Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain, primarily aimed at stealing intellectual property to bolster China's AI chip self-sufficiency. Researchers identified at least three distinct groups—UNK_FistBump, UNK_DropPitch, and UNK_SparkyCarp—using sophisticated spear-phishing and malware, such as the "Voldemort" backdoor, against 15–20 organizations, including manufacturers, designers, and testing facilities.

In March 2025, a new strain of destructive malware called PathWiper (linked to the group ELECTRUM) was detected across manufacturing sectors in Eastern Europe. Unlike ransomware, which encrypts data for a fee, PathWiper is a "wiper" designed for irreversible destruction. It overwrites the Master Boot Record (MBR) and NTFS metadata of factory floor servers. Total loss of historical production data and machine configuration files. It was described as "digital arson," designed to maximize the time needed to rebuild production lines from scratch, rather than extracting a ransom.

The breaches were linked to a wider campaign by the ShinyHunters extortion group (associated with Scattered Spider), targeting Salesforce instances via social engineering to steal customer names, contact details, and purchase histories.

Verified Impact Summary: On March 11, 2026, medical technology giant Stryker suffered a major cyberattack by the Handala hacker group, an Iran-linked entity, disrupting manufacturing, shipping, and order processing across 79 countries. The attackers used a destructive "wiper" technique to disrupt over 200,000 Microsoft-based systems and mobile devices, causing global disruptions for the Fortune 500 company.

In late March 2026, the global defense giant Lockheed Martin was targeted by a group tracked as APT Iran (likely an auxiliary persona for state-linked operations). The group claimed to have exfiltrated 375 terabytes of sensitive data, including F-35 aircraft blueprints and technical specs for advanced missile systems. While the full investigation is ongoing, initial reports suggest the group used a combination of credential stuffing (leveraging passwords leaked from previous third-party breaches) and the exploitation of a zero-day in a high-speed file transfer protocol used for large engineering datasets. Beyond the potential loss of strategic military secrets, the breach triggered an immediate global security audit across all Lockheed subcontractors, highlighting the extreme risk in the defense industrial base.

The German chemical giant BASF was hit by a targeted ransomware attack from a group calling itself 0apt in early February 2026. Unlike general ransomware, this attack was surgically aimed at chemical catalyst formulas and factory automation code (PLCs). The attackers bypassed traditional perimeter defenses by compromising a service account used by an outsourced industrial maintenance firm. This allowed them to move laterally directly into the Manufacturing Execution System (MES). BASF reported that while safety systems remained intact, proprietary production "recipes" were accessed. The incident emphasized a new trend: IP-centric extortion, where the threat isn't just locking systems, but selling specialized chemical "blueprints" to global competitors.

This is the most significant industrial event of the current year. Six U.S. federal agencies (including CISA and the FBI) issued an emergency warning regarding an Iranian-linked group, CyberAv3ngers. The group targeted internet-connected Rockwell Automation / Allen-Bradley PLCs (specifically the CompactLogix and Micro850 lines). They didn't use complex malware; they used legitimate engineering software (Studio 5000 Logix Designer) to connect to exposed controllers and manipulate the "Human Machine Interface" (HMI) displays.

Reports from March 2026 indicate a 300% surge in "reconnaissance-only" attacks against the Taiwanese semiconductor ecosystem. Unlike ransomware, these attacks (linked to state-aligned groups like Volt Typhoon) do not encrypt files. Instead, they embed "sleeper" malware in the firmware of industrial switches. The goal is "pre-positioning"—establishing a foothold so that they can trigger a global chip shortage at a moment's notice during a geopolitical crisis.

FrostyGoop (disclosed 2023–2024) is the ninth known ICS-specific malware, and is unique for exploiting the common Modbus PLC protocol to directly issue malicious commands. Written in Go, it was used in an attack on Ukrainian city infrastructure (heating system) in early 2024 that turned off boilers, showing its ability to manipulate control outputs and change device parameters. FrostyGoop’s design is somewhat simpler than earlier state malware—it leverages open-source libraries and straightforward read/write commands—yet it represents the continued evolution of ICS threats beyond elite state actors. By using Modbus (a widely deployed protocol) for C2 and payload actions, FrostyGoop demonstrates how attackers are broadening their toolkit to target industrial devices directly via standard channels. Its appearance underscores a trend toward more accessible ICS attack methods (potentially available to cybercriminals or hacktivists) while still having significant impact on operations (in this case, leaving civilians without heat in winter).
Source / Verification URL: MITRE ATT&CK; Dragos report; Wired; SecurityWeek
